before: Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?”
after: Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what should we do?”
ground: Convicted hearers seek the apostles' ruling on the response they ought to make, so the force is obligation and takes 'should'.

before: I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ The Lord said to me, ‘Arise, and go into Damascus. There you will be told about all things which are appointed for you to do.’
after: I said, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ The Lord said to me, ‘Arise, and go into Damascus. There you will be told about all things which are appointed for you to do.’
ground: Paul surrenders his course to the Lord's direction and asks what he ought to do, so the force is obligation and takes 'should'.

before: What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?
after: What do you want? Will I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?
ground: Paul puts the manner of his own future coming to the readers' choice ('What do you want?'), an open course of intention, so it takes 'will'.

before: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
after: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often should my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
ground: Peter asks how often the duty of forgiveness binds him, an obligation question, so it takes 'should'.

before: See, one came to him and said, “Good teacher, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?”
after: See, one came to him and said, “Good teacher, what good thing should I do, that I may have eternal life?”
ground: The man asks what good thing he ought to do to have eternal life, an obligation question seeking instruction, so it takes 'should'.

before: She went out and said to her mother, “What shall I ask?” She said, “The head of John the Baptizer.”
after: She went out and said to her mother, “What should I ask?” She said, “The head of John the Baptizer.”
ground: The daughter seeks her mother's ruling on what she ought to request, an obligation question, so it takes 'should'.

before: As he was going out into the way, one ran to him, knelt before him, and asked him, “Good Teacher, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?”
after: As he was going out into the way, one ran to him, knelt before him, and asked him, “Good Teacher, what should I do that I may inherit eternal life?”
ground: The man asks what he ought to do to inherit eternal life, an obligation question seeking instruction, so it takes 'should'.

before: See, a certain lawyer stood up and tested him, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
after: See, a certain lawyer stood up and tested him, saying, “Teacher, what should I do to inherit eternal life?”
ground: The lawyer asks what he ought to do to inherit eternal life, an obligation question seeking instruction, so it takes 'should'.

before: A certain ruler asked him, saying, “Good Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
after: A certain ruler asked him, saying, “Good Teacher, what should I do to inherit eternal life?”
ground: The ruler asks what he ought to do to inherit eternal life, an obligation question seeking instruction, so it takes 'should'.

before: The lord of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son. It may be that seeing him, they will respect him.’
after: The lord of the vineyard said, ‘What will I do? I will send my beloved son. It may be that seeing him, they will respect him.’
ground: The owner's soliloquy settles on his own next act in the same breath ('I will send my beloved son'), an open course of intention, so it takes 'will'.

before: What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
after: What will we say then? Should we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
ground: Judged with its built-in answer ('May it never be'): the first question is Paul's self-answered speech transition, the same formula the base itself gives in 'will' at Romans 3:5 and 4:1, so it takes 'will'; the second asks whether continuing in sin is permissible, an obligation question refused in the same breath, so it takes 'should'.

before: What then? Shall we sin because we are not under law but under grace? May it never be!
after: What then? Should we sin because we are not under law but under grace? May it never be!
ground: Judged with its built-in answer in the same verse ('May it never be!'): the question asks whether sinning is permissible, an obligation question, so it takes 'should'.

before: What shall we say then? Is the law sin? May it never be! However, I wouldn’t have known sin except through the law. For I wouldn’t have known coveting unless the law had said, “You must not covet.”
after: What will we say then? Is the law sin? May it never be! However, I wouldn’t have known sin except through the law. For I wouldn’t have known coveting unless the law had said, “You must not covet.”
ground: The first 'shall' is Paul's self-answered speech-formula transition, the same formula the base itself gives in 'will' at Romans 3:5 and 4:1, so it takes 'will' (the verse's quoted commandment 'You must not covet' is untouched).

before: What then shall we say about these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?
after: What then will we say about these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?
ground: Paul's self-answered speech-formula transition stating what the argument will say next, the same formula the base itself gives in 'will' at Romans 3:5 and 4:1, so it takes 'will'.

before: What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? May it never be!
after: What will we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? May it never be!
ground: Paul's self-answered speech-formula transition, answered at once with 'May it never be!', the same formula the base itself gives in 'will' at Romans 3:5 and 4:1, so it takes 'will'.

before: What shall we say then? That the Gentiles, who didn’t follow after righteousness, attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith;
after: What will we say then? That the Gentiles, who didn’t follow after righteousness, attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith;
ground: Paul's speech-formula transition whose conclusion he himself states as its continuation, the same formula the base itself gives in 'will' at Romans 3:5 and 4:1, so it takes 'will'.

before: Don’t you know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? May it never be!
after: Don’t you know that your bodies are members of Christ? Should I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? May it never be!
ground: Judged with its built-in refusal in the same verse ('May it never be!'): Paul asks whether the act would be permissible, an obligation question, so it takes 'should'.

before: What, don’t you have houses to eat and to drink in? Or do you despise God’s assembly and put them to shame who don’t have enough? What shall I tell you? Shall I praise you? In this I don’t praise you.
after: What, don’t you have houses to eat and to drink in? Or do you despise God’s assembly and put them to shame who don’t have enough? What will I tell you? Should I praise you? In this I don’t praise you.
ground: Judged as one unit with Paul's self-supplied answer ('In this I don't praise you'): the first question is his open next act of speech, so it takes 'will'; the second asks whether praise is warranted, an obligation question he answers in the negative, so it takes 'should'.

before: What more shall I say? For the time would fail me if I told of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets—
after: What more will I say? For the time would fail me if I told of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets—
ground: The author's self-answered speech transition, answered by the roll of names that follows, an open course of speech, so it takes 'will'.

before: Furthermore, we had the fathers of our flesh to chasten us, and we paid them respect. Shall we not much rather be in subjection to the Father of spirits and live?
after: Furthermore, we had the fathers of our flesh to chasten us, and we paid them respect. Should we not much rather be in subjection to the Father of spirits and live?
ground: Judged with the a fortiori argument of verses 9-10: as earthly fathers were respected, so much more ought the readers be in subjection to the Father of spirits, an obligation force, so it takes 'should'.

before: “But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces, who call to their companions
after: “But to what will I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces, who call to their companions
ground: Jesus chooses the comparison he will make, an open course of speech (the Mark 4:30 parallel stands in the base's own 'will'), so it takes 'will'.

before: But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” They asked him, “Shall we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give them something to eat?”
after: But he answered them, “You give them something to eat.” They asked him, “Should we go and buy two hundred denarii worth of bread and give them something to eat?”
ground: The disciples put a proposed purchase up to Jesus as the decision-maker, asking whether they ought to go and buy, an obligation proposal, so it takes 'should'.

before: Jesus answered, “Faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.”
after: Jesus answered, “Faithless and perverse generation, how long will I be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.”
ground: The lament asks how long Jesus's own presence and bearing will continue, a future-duration course and not an ought (the Mark 9:19 parallel stands converted to 'will'), so it takes 'will'.

before: He said, “What is God’s Kingdom like? To what shall I compare it?
after: He said, “What is God’s Kingdom like? To what will I compare it?
ground: Jesus chooses the comparison he will make, an open course of speech (the Mark 4:30 parallel stands in the base's own 'will'), so it takes 'will'.

before: Again he said, “To what shall I compare God’s Kingdom?
after: Again he said, “To what will I compare God’s Kingdom?
ground: Jesus chooses the comparison he will make, an open course of speech (the Mark 4:30 parallel stands in the base's own 'will'), so it takes 'will'.

before: When those who were around him saw what was about to happen, they said to him, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?”
after: When those who were around him saw what was about to happen, they said to him, “Lord, should we strike with the sword?”
ground: The disciples seek the Lord's ruling before acting, asking whether they ought to strike with the sword, an obligation question, so it takes 'should'.
